extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning discrete mathematics / relations
extracted.subtask_description: Understand, represent, and determine properties of binary relations (from A to B or on A): composition, inverse, domain/range, reflexive/symmetric/transitive, orders, bounds, and related proofs or counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation (from A to B) / notation xRy
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R from A to B is a set of ordered pairs (subset of A x B). If R is a relation from A to B, x ∈ A, and y ∈ B, then mathematicians sometimes write xRy to mean (x,y) ∈ R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative viewpoints (set of ordered pairs, notation xRy) and multiple representations (ordered-pair list, picture) are equivalent. Examples: student s lives in dorm room r written sLr meaning (s,r) ∈ L.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of relations (S o R)
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is a relation from A to B and S is a relation from B to C, then S o R = {(a,c) ∈ A x C | ∃ b ∈ B (aRb and bSc)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret composition as a two-step path: (a,c) is in S o R iff you can get from a to c in two steps. Use pictures (directed graphs) to visualize composition (follow an arrow from a to b and from b to c). Example: students-courses-professors E and T give T o E pairs (student,professor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain and Range (Dom(R), Ran(R))
rubrics_metrics.description: Domain of R consists of elements in A that appear as first coordinates of pairs in R; range consists of elements in B that appear as second coordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In directed-graph pictures, domain = vertices in A with edges pointing away; range = vertices in B with edges pointing toward them. Example: for R = {(1,3),(1,5),(3,3)}, Dom(R) = {1,3}, Ran(R) = {3,5}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed-graph picture of a relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent elements of domain and codomain as vertices (dots) in ovals and ordered pairs as directed edges (arrows) from the first component to the second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loops (edge from a vertex to itself) represent (x,x) ∈ R. Location of vertices is irrelevant; edges must correspond exactly to ordered pairs. Useful for visualizing domain, range, composition (paths).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity relation i_A
rubrics_metrics.description: i_A = {(x,x) | x ∈ A}, sometimes called the identity relation on A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: i_A is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. It acts as the identity for composition: for relations R from A to B, i_B o R = R and R o i_A = R (exercise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflexive relation
rubrics_metrics.description: R is reflexive on A if ∀x ∈ A (x R x), equivalently ∀x ∈ A ((x,x) ∈ R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Picture criterion: loops at all vertices. Algebraic equivalent (Theorem 4.3.4(1)): R is reflexive iff i_A ⊆ R. Examples: identity relation i_A is reflexive; D_r = {(x,y) | |x-y| < r} is reflexive since |x-x|=0<r.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric relation
rubrics_metrics.description: R is symmetric if ∀x ∈ A ∀y ∈ A (xRy ⇒ yRx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Picture criterion: every non-loop edge comes paired with the reverse edge. Algebraic equivalent (Theorem 4.3.4(2)): R is symmetric iff R = R^{-1}. Examples: D_r (|x-y| < r) is symmetric; > is not symmetric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitive relation
rubrics_metrics.description: R is transitive if ∀x,y,z ∈ A ((xRy ∧ yRz) ⇒ xRz).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition criterion (Theorem 4.3.4(3)): R is transitive iff R o R ⊆ R. Picture interpretation: whenever there is a path x→y→z, there must be a direct edge x→z. Examples: > on ℝ is transitive; D_r is not transitive (explicit counterexample using points spaced 2r/3 apart).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse relation R^{-1}
rubrics_metrics.description: R^{-1} (denoted R^−1 or R^! in the text) is obtained by reversing ordered pairs: (x,y) ∈ R ⇔ (y,x) ∈ R^{-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interchanges domain and range; pictorially reverses arrow directions. Used in equivalences: R symmetric ⇔ R = R^{-1}. If R is reflexive/symmetric/transitive then certain closures/invariants under inverse hold (exercises ask to prove/refute).

rubrics_metrics.name: Loop
rubrics_metrics.description: An edge from a vertex to itself in the directed graph, representing (x,x) ∈ R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of loops at all vertices indicates reflexivity. Single loops may occur even if relation not reflexive overall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antisymmetric relation
rubrics_metrics.description: R is antisymmetric if ∀x ∈ A ∀y ∈ A ((xRy ∧ yRx) ⇒ x = y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means there are no distinct x and y with edges in both directions. Examples: subset relation ⊆ on P(A) is antisymmetric; relation '>' is antisymmetric in the sense of its definition of ordering? (Used to define partial orders.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial order
rubrics_metrics.description: R is a partial order on A if it is reflexive, transitive, and antisymmetric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial orders model 'at least as large as' relations but need not compare all pairs. Examples: subset ⊆ on P(A), divisibility on positive integers. Visualization: Hasse diagrams (directed graphs without all transitive edges) are commonly used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total order (linear order)
rubrics_metrics.description: R is a total order on A if it is a partial order and additionally ∀x,y ∈ A (xRy ∨ yRx) (comparability of every pair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Total orders compare every pair. Example: < on ℝ is a total order (the text's L). Many partial orders (like ⊆ on P(A)) are not total.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smallest element (in a subset B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given R a partial order on A and B ⊆ A, b ∈ B is R-smallest in B if ∀x ∈ B (b R x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A smallest element (if it exists) is unique (Theorem 4.4.6(1)). A smallest element is also the unique minimal element. Example: 7 is smallest of B = {x ∈ ℝ | x ≥ 7} under < (with 7 ∈ B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal element (in a subset B)
rubrics_metrics.description: b ∈ B is R-minimal if ¬∃ x ∈ B (x R b ∧ x ≠ b). Equivalently ∀x ∈ B (x R b ⇒ x = b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimal does not imply smallest in general partial orders (only in total orders by Theorem 4.4.6(3)). Example: set C = {a, me, men, tame, mental} under substring-order has minimal elements 'a' and 'me' but no smallest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Largest / Maximal elements
rubrics_metrics.description: b ∈ B is largest if ∀x ∈ B (x R b). b is maximal in B if ¬∃ x ∈ B (b R x ∧ b ≠ x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Largest is unique if it exists; maximal may not be unique. These are dual notions to smallest/minimal. Exercises explore their properties and relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower bound and upper bound
rubrics_metrics.description: For R a partial order on A and B ⊆ A, a ∈ A is a lower bound for B if ∀x ∈ B (a R x). Similarly, a is an upper bound for B if ∀x ∈ B (x R a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lower/upper bound need not belong to B (difference from smallest/largest). Example: 7 is a lower bound (greatest lower bound) for C = {x ∈ ℝ | x > 7} though 7 ∉ C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Least upper bound (l.u.b.) and greatest lower bound (g.l.b.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let U be the set of all upper bounds of B; if U has a smallest element it is the least upper bound. Let L be set of lower bounds; if L has a largest element it is the greatest lower bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviations l.u.b. and g.l.b. Example: for B = {1/n | n ∈ ℕ*}, l.u.b. = 1, greatest lower bound = 0 (example in text shows l.u.b. existence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalences linking properties to set operations (Theorem 4.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem statements: (1) R reflexive iff i_A ⊆ R. (2) R symmetric iff R = R^{-1}. (3) R transitive iff R o R ⊆ R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These give alternate algebraic/set-based formulations useful for proofs. The text demonstrates proof strategies (element-chasing, arbitrary-element method) and leaves some parts as exercises for practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and identity interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: For relations R from A to B, properties like i_B o R = R and R o i_A = R hold (exercise asks to show). Also RoR ⊆ R is the transitivity test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use identity relation as neutral element for composition; these equalities are standard and used in algebraic manipulation of relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure / preservation questions for union, intersection, composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Are reflexivity/symmetry/transitivity preserved under union, intersection, composition (and set difference)? The text poses many parts asking for proofs or counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some general facts: union/intersection of reflexive relations is reflexive (since i_A is subset of each); intersection of transitive relations is transitive; union of transitive relations need not be transitive. The page encourages either proof or exhibiting counterexample for each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lifting relations to P(A) / quantifier pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: When defining a relation S on P(A) from a relation R on A via quantified conditions (e.g. S = {(X,Y) | ∃ x∈X ∃ y∈Y xRy} or other quantifier patterns), transitivity/reflexivity/symmetry may or may not lift; proofs that rely on picking 'an x ∈ X' may be invalid if X can be empty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives a putative (flawed) proof and asks to identify the error, and shows that excluding the empty set can be necessary for some lifts to hold. Always watch quantifier order and the presence of empty sets when lifting properties from elements to subsets.
